vignette:
He is 78 and still introduces himself, with a kind of dry precision, as a database administrator, though retirement has been on paper for years. In practice, he remains the person family members call when a password is forgotten, a backup fails, or a tax document needs finding. He likes systems that can be checked, restored, and made to make sense. That preference, he says, used to feel like a professional habit. Since his illness, it feels like a necessity.

The traumatic period begins with what he first assumes is a minor medical problem. He notices fatigue, then a vague tightness in his chest, a strange shortness of breath when he walks from the parking lot to the office. He tells himself to slow down. He has always been careful, methodical, and he dislikes making a fuss. For a while, he keeps working. He sits at his desk, eyes moving across lines of code and rows of data, telling himself that if he can still focus, then he is probably all right. But the body does not cooperate with his logic. The weakness worsens. He grows lightheaded. A routine appointment becomes urgent, then alarming, and then he is in a hospital bed hearing words he cannot quite absorb all at once.

The illness is life-threatening, and he understands that fact in fragments. He remembers the change in the room when the doctors begin speaking more slowly, more carefully. He remembers his own sudden attention to their faces, the way he watches for signs that they are hiding something. He hears probabilities, procedures, risks. He is stunned by how quickly he moves from managing his own calendar to surrendering it to other people. Tests, scans, consultations, interventions: his days become a sequence of decisions made under pressure. He says that at one point he feels as if he has been handed a report with missing pages and told to trust the conclusion anyway.

During the worst days, he develops a constant readiness for disaster. He listens for footsteps in the hallway. He startles when a phone rings. At night, he lies awake and monitors his own breathing, convinced that if he sleeps too deeply, something will stop. He develops a habit of counting the minutes between sensations in his chest, mentally checking and rechecking his pulse, as if vigilance alone might keep him alive. He describes the hospital as a place where time becomes jagged. A nurse’s expression, a monitor’s beep, a sharp turn in a conversation can send him into a wave of dread. He feels trapped inside a body he no longer trusts.

After discharge, he expects relief, but the fear follows him home. He returns to his apartment alone, having been divorced for many years, and the quiet there feels less peaceful than exposed. He keeps the television on because silence makes him listen too closely to his breathing. He sleeps in short stretches and wakes with his heart racing. At times he smells antiseptic where none is present or feels a rush of panic when he sees a medical bill in the mail. He avoids the route to the clinic and postpones follow-up appointments until the last possible moment. He remains compliant, in his own words, but compliance is now accompanied by dread. Each appointment can turn into a countdown.

He also notices how the illness has altered his sense of himself. He was once proud of being dependable, the person who kept systems running. Now he mistrusts his memory and concentration. He rereads emails three or four times. He loses track of conversations. When a database query takes longer than expected, he feels a flash of irritability and then shame, as if his old competence were slipping away. He often thinks about the day his body first failed him and wonders whether he missed some warning that a more attentive man would have caught. The self-reproach comes easily; reassurance does not.

He still functions, but narrowly. He shops early to avoid crowds and fatigue. He keeps medications lined up in a precise order on the kitchen counter. He makes lists for errands that he used to hold in his head. Even on better days, he carries a sense that danger is nearby and only partly visible. He is not the dramatic kind of frightened man; he is careful, contained, and matter-of-fact. Yet beneath that steadiness there is a persistent alertness, a body braced for bad news, a mind that continues to return to the hospital room and the feeling that his life had been hanging by a thread he could not see.
